title: What is inflation?
body: Inflation is a general rise in prices over time, so each unit of money buys less. It is often measured with a consumer price index (CPI), which tracks the cost of a typical basket of goods and services.

title: Supply and demand
body: When demand for something rises and supply stays the same, its price tends to rise. When supply rises and demand stays the same, the price tends to fall. The price where the two meet is called the equilibrium.

title: What GDP measures
body: Gross domestic product (GDP) is the total market value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a given period, usually a year or a quarter. It is the most common measure of the size of an economy.

title: GDP per person
body: GDP per capita divides GDP by the population. It is a rough guide to average living standards, but it hides inequality: a few very rich people can raise the average while most people's incomes stay low.

title: Opportunity cost
body: The opportunity cost of a choice is the value of the next best alternative you give up. If you spend an evening working overtime, the opportunity cost might be time with family. Every choice has one.

title: What central banks do
body: A central bank manages a country's currency and money supply. One of its main tools is the interest rate: raising rates makes borrowing more expensive, which tends to slow spending and inflation.

title: Comparative advantage
body: Countries gain from trade when each specialises in what it produces at a lower opportunity cost than others, even if one country is better at everything. The idea is linked to the economist David Ricardo (1817).

title: Zimbabwe's hyperinflation
body: In 2008 Zimbabwe experienced one of the worst hyperinflations in history, with prices doubling roughly every day at its peak. The central bank printed a 100 trillion dollar note. The currency was abandoned in 2009.

title: What is a recession?
body: A recession is a significant, widespread fall in economic activity. A common rule of thumb is two consecutive quarters of falling GDP, though official bodies look at wider data such as jobs and incomes.

title: Exchange rates
body: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another. When your currency weakens, imports cost more but your exports become cheaper for foreign buyers.

title: What is a tariff?
body: A tariff is a tax on imported goods. Governments use tariffs to raise money or protect local industries, but they usually make imported goods more expensive for consumers and can lead to retaliation.

title: Trade surplus and deficit
body: The balance of trade is a country's exports minus its imports. If it exports more than it imports, it has a trade surplus. If it imports more, it has a trade deficit.

title: Measuring unemployment
body: The unemployment rate is the share of people in the labour force who have no job but are available and looking for work. People not looking for work, such as full-time students, are not counted as unemployed.

title: What is a monopoly?
body: A monopoly exists when one company is the only seller of a product with no close substitutes. Without competition it can charge higher prices, which is why many countries have competition laws.

title: Price elasticity
body: Price elasticity of demand measures how much buying changes when price changes. Demand for essentials like salt barely changes (inelastic); demand for luxuries or items with substitutes changes a lot (elastic).

title: Scarcity
body: Scarcity is the basic economic problem: human wants are unlimited, but resources such as land, labour, time and money are limited. So people, businesses and governments must make choices.

title: The Wealth of Nations
body: Adam Smith published 'The Wealth of Nations' in 1776. It argued that division of labour and free markets create wealth, and introduced the famous 'invisible hand' idea. It is often called the first modern work of economics.

title: Fiscal and monetary policy
body: Fiscal policy is government spending and taxation, decided by the government and parliament. Monetary policy is control of interest rates and money supply, usually by the central bank. Both are used to steady the economy.

title: What is deflation?
body: Deflation is a general fall in prices. It sounds good, but it can be harmful: people delay purchases expecting lower prices, businesses earn less, and debts become harder to repay.

title: The euro
body: The euro was introduced as an electronic currency on 1 January 1999. Euro banknotes and coins entered circulation on 1 January 2002, replacing currencies such as the German mark and French franc.

title: Africa's free trade area
body: The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) began trading on 1 January 2021. It aims to create a single market for goods and services across Africa by gradually removing tariffs between member states.
source_name: Wikipedia: African Continental Free Trade Area

title: The informal economy
body: The informal economy is economic activity that is not taxed or regulated by government, such as many street traders and small unregistered businesses. In many developing countries it employs most workers.

title: Government debt
body: Government debt is the total a government owes from past borrowing. It is often compared with GDP (debt-to-GDP ratio) to judge how affordable it is. Interest on debt competes with spending on schools and hospitals.

title: Externalities
body: An externality is a cost or benefit that affects people outside a transaction. Pollution from a factory is a negative externality; a neighbour's beautiful garden is a positive one. Taxes and rules are used to correct them.

title: Economics word: stagflation
body: Meaning: high inflation combined with slow growth and high unemployment at the same time.
example_sentence: The oil shocks of the 1970s caused stagflation in many countries.

title: Economics word: austerity
body: Meaning: government policies that cut spending or raise taxes to reduce a budget deficit.
example_sentence: The austerity budget cut funding for public projects.

title: Economics word: subsidy
body: Meaning: money given by government to lower the cost of a product or support an industry.
example_sentence: A fuel subsidy keeps petrol prices lower than their market level.

title: Economics word: commodity
body: Meaning: a basic good that is traded and largely the same whoever produces it, such as oil, copper, coffee or maize.
example_sentence: Copper is Zambia's most important export commodity.

title: Economics word: productivity
body: Meaning: how much output is produced per worker or per hour of work.
example_sentence: New machines raised the factory's productivity by 20%.

title: Economics word: liquidity
body: Meaning: how quickly and easily an asset can be turned into cash without losing value.
example_sentence: Cash has perfect liquidity; a house has very little.

title: Rising prices
body: Definitions check.
statement: Inflation means prices in general are rising
explanation: Inflation is a general, sustained rise in prices, so money buys less over time.

title: Demand goes up
body: Supply and demand.
statement: If demand rises and supply stays the same, prices usually fall
explanation: More buyers chasing the same amount of goods pushes prices up.

title: Measuring an economy
body: Definitions check.
statement: GDP measures the value of goods and services a country produces in a period
explanation: GDP is the total market value of final goods and services produced in a country in a given period.

title: Taxing imports
body: Trade check.
statement: A tariff is a tax on imported goods
explanation: Tariffs are taxes on imports, which raise their price in the local market.

title: Printing money
body: Money check.
statement: Printing lots of new money always makes a country richer
explanation: More money chasing the same goods raises prices. Zimbabwe in 2008 is an extreme example.

title: Trade deficit
body: Trade check.
statement: A trade deficit means a country imports more than it exports
explanation: Exports minus imports is negative when imports are larger. That gap is the trade deficit.

title: What deflation means
body: Definitions check.
statement: Deflation means prices are rising quickly
explanation: Deflation is a general fall in prices. Fast rising prices are high inflation.

title: The cost of a choice
body: Key concept.
statement: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative you give up
explanation: Choosing one thing means not choosing another. The best option you gave up is the opportunity cost.

title: Fighting inflation
body: Central banks.
statement: Central banks often raise interest rates to fight high inflation
explanation: Higher rates make borrowing more expensive, which cools spending and slows price rises.

title: Euro cash
body: History check.
statement: Euro banknotes and coins entered circulation in 2002
explanation: The euro existed electronically from 1999; notes and coins arrived on 1 January 2002.

title: The Phillips curve
body: In the 1950s and 60s, lower unemployment seemed to come with higher inflation. The 1970s broke that simple trade-off when stagflation brought both at once. Today it is seen as a short-run relationship that depends on expectations.

title: The multiplier effect
body: When a government spends 100 on a road, workers spend part of their wages, which becomes other people's income, and so on. GDP can rise by more than 100. The more of each extra dollar people save or spend on imports, the smaller the multiplier.

title: Gresham's law
body: Bad money drives out good: when two currencies are officially equal but trusted differently, people spend the weaker one and hoard the stronger. Zimbabweans saw this when US dollars were saved while bond notes were spent.

title: Nash equilibrium
body: A Nash equilibrium is a set of choices where no player gains by changing only their own strategy. It explains price wars and arms races, and why cartels such as OPEC struggle to stop members producing more than agreed.
